analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover addiction treatment on equal terms with medical care.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a Senate vote: it was referred to the Senate Health committee in July 1999 and never acted on before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar health plans from setting stricter limits — higher copays, fewer visits, lower dollar caps — on drug and alcohol addiction treatment than they set for other medical care. It applies to group plans and individual insurance, but only to employers with more than 25 workers, and it does not force any plan to offer addiction treatment benefits at all. It was referred to the Senate Health committee and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private health insurance who need treatment for drug or alcohol addiction. If a plan offers substance abuse treatment today, it can still cap the number of covered days, charge higher coinsurance, and impose lower dollar limits than it applies to other care; the bill would prohibit that unequal treatment. Workers at large employers, whose plans cover most insured Americans, would benefit most, since small employers are exempt.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People needing drug or alcohol addiction treatment

how_it_helps.text: Bars group health plans and individual-market insurance from imposing treatment limits or cost-sharing on substance abuse treatment unless the same limits apply to medical and surgical benefits [S2][S3].
Covers the full range of treatment — inpatient detoxification, residential programs, outpatient counseling, medication management, and prevention services [S3].
Lets states keep stronger protections than the federal floor requires [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and large employers, who would face higher claims costs when addiction treatment is covered on equal terms, potentially passed to premiums. Workers at small employers (25 or fewer employees) get nothing, because those employers are exempt.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not require any plan to offer substance abuse treatment benefits at all — a plan could avoid the parity rule simply by dropping the benefit [S3].
Small employers with 25 or fewer employees are exempt, leaving their workers without the protection [S2][S3].
Coverage on equal terms would raise claims costs for insurers and employers, which could show up as higher premiums for everyone in a plan.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of workers whose plans cover addiction treatment but wall it off with harsher limits than other care, equal treatment is a real, concrete benefit at the moment they need care most. The cost is higher premiums spread across all enrollees, and the design has real gaps: plans can escape by dropping the benefit, and small-firm workers are left out entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Wellstone introduced the bill on July 28, 1999, joined by original cosponsors Kennedy, Inouye, Daschle, and Moynihan [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1][S5].
No further action was recorded; the bill never reached the Senate floor and expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers were spared the cost of covering addiction treatment on equal terms, while people with substance abuse problems kept facing the stricter limits and higher cost-sharing the bill would have prohibited.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers; untreated patients were not

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as sponsor.

for.name: Sens. Kennedy, Inouye, Daschle, and Moynihan
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled action on it, keeping it from the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Democrat with a small bipartisan cosponsor group (5 Democrats, 1 Republican), and no votes were ever taken, so the partisan split of the full chamber was never tested.

industries.note: Parity would raise their claims costs by forcing equal coverage of addiction treatment where a plan offers it — though the bill's loophole lets a plan drop the benefit entirely to escape. The bill never became law, so insurers bore nothing.
Equal coverage terms would have meant more patients able to use insurance for detox, residential, and outpatient care, with less imposed cost-sharing.
Employers with more than 25 employees would have absorbed higher benefit costs; small employers were exempted.
